subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

section_titles: Line of symmetry and mirror line
periods.activity_title: Fold, Press, Unfold — Ink Designs and Symmetry

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 1. Ink Design, p.164
tasks_in_class.description: Fold a sheet of paper in half, sprinkle water-colour drops at the fold, press to spread colour, open and observe the symmetrical ink design produced.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (a)–(c), p.165
tasks_in_class.description: Mark the line of symmetry in Fig. 3, 4, and 5; count how many lines of symmetry Fig. 8 has; decide where to place a mirror to see the right-half reflection and whether it matches the left half.

time_bands.activity: Each child folds a sheet in half, drops water-colour at the fold, presses the paper shut, and opens it: Let Us Do, 1. Ink Design, p.164 ("Fold … open and observe the symmetrical ink design…"). Children describe what they see — two halves that match — and the teacher names the fold-line as the line of symmetry.

Children fold a sheet through the first three steps of the paper-airplane sequence and, at each fold, draw the line of symmetry on the flap. For part (c): Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (a)–(c), p.165 ("Mark the line of symmetry in Fig. 3, 4, and 5…."). The class discusses where a mirror placed on the finished airplane would show the right half, and whether the reflection matches the left.

Pairs share their marked airplanes and count how many lines of symmetry Fig. 8 has. The teacher introduces the term 'mirror line' as the vocabulary upgrade for line of symmetry, writing both names on the board and inviting children to say when each feels natural.

Quick circle discussion: children hold up their ink-design papers and point to the mirror line. Teacher invites one or two to say in their own words what the fold-line does to both halves, anchoring the definition before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: Children arriving at this unit from the rangoli and mask symmetry they saw in Grade 3 will find the ink-blot activity a vivid reintroduction. A common error is marking two lines on a shape that has only one: the airplane folds clarify that a line of symmetry must divide the shape so each half is an exact reflection of the other. Keep small mirrors available so children can check their marked lines by placing the mirror on the fold and verifying the hidden half appears.
materials: Plain white paper (one sheet per child)

section_titles: Line of symmetry and mirror line
Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
periods.activity_title: Flying Asymmetry and First Fold-and-Cut Challenges

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (d)–(h), p.165
tasks_in_class.description: Fly the symmetrical plane; try making an asymmetrical plane; fly both and observe which flies longer; share observations with friends.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, p.166
tasks_in_class.description: Take a square sheet of paper; fold and cut to reproduce Mini's design (fold twice, straight corner cut + two side squares removed).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 1, p.166
tasks_in_class.description: Predict where the hole and cut will appear when Rani's twice-folded paper (corner cut + two side squares) is opened.

time_bands.activity: Children complete their paper airplanes and fly the symmetrical version across an open space. They then deliberately fold one wing differently to make an asymmetrical plane and fly it: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (d)–(h), p.165 ("Fly the symmetrical plane … observe which flies longer…."). Pairs record which plane flew further and discuss why symmetry might help flight.

Transition to fold-and-cut. Each child takes a square sheet, folds it twice as described, makes a straight corner cut and removes two side squares to reproduce Mini's design: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, p.166 ("fold twice, straight corner cut + two side squares removed…"). Children open the paper and name what they see.

Challenge 1: before cutting, children draw a quick sketch predicting where the hole and cut will appear in Rani's twice-folded paper: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 1, p.166 ("Predict where the hole and cut will appear…."). They then cut and open to check. Pairs compare predictions with results and explain any difference.

Class share-out: teacher holds up two or three predicted sketches alongside the opened results. Children articulate what the double fold does to a single cut — a guided inductive moment connecting the fold-and-cut experience to the mirror-line idea from the ink-blot and airplane work.

periods.teacher_notes: The flight comparison anchors an inquiry question children can reason about with concrete evidence before moving into the more abstract fold-and-cut work. A frequent spatial error in Challenge 1 is predicting that a corner cut makes one hole rather than four: remind children to trace mentally what the folded layers look like when opened. Square sheets of roughly equal size make the comparison across groups reliable.
materials: Open space or corridor for the airplane flight

section_titles: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
periods.activity_title: Predict, Cut, Count — Fold-and-Cut Challenges 2 and 3

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 2, p.166
tasks_in_class.description: Fold a piece of paper once; put two cuts in the middle as shown. How many sides will the shape have when you open the folded paper?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 3, p.166
tasks_in_class.description: Fold a paper twice. Where would you cut to make a square hole in the centre? How many cuts are required?

time_bands.activity: Children briefly revisit the outcome of Challenge 1 by holding their opened sheets from the previous unit and recounting what the double fold did to a corner cut. This naming-the-content recap takes the form of a quick show-and-tell, not a retelling of what happened in another sitting.

Challenge 2: each child folds a sheet once and, before cutting, sketches a prediction of how many sides the opened shape will have after two mid-cuts: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 2, p.166 ("Fold … two cuts in the middle … how many sides when opened?…"). Children count sides on their sketch, then cut, open, and count again. Groups of three compare counts and resolve disagreements.

Challenge 3: children fold a fresh sheet twice and mark with pencil where they think one cut should go to produce a square hole in the centre: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 3, p.166 ("Where would you cut to make a square hole … how many cuts required?…"). They cut, open, and examine whether the hole is centred and square. Pairs discuss why a single cut on a twice-folded sheet produces four edges.
A one-minute class debrief: teacher asks children to say in one phrase what a double fold does to a single cut. Responses are a formative gauge of spatial reasoning before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have worked with fold-and-cut spatial reasoning in Mini's design and Challenge 1 bring that concrete experience to bear here on increasingly open-ended predictions. The most common error in Challenge 2 is miscounting sides by treating the fold-edge as a separate side; encourage children to trace each edge with a finger after opening. For Challenge 3, children who struggle may need to mark the centre of the folded paper before deciding where to cut.

section_titles: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
periods.activity_title: Dot-Grid Shapes and Mirror Games with Real Mirrors

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, Symmetry in shapes Q1, p.167
tasks_in_class.description: Draw the border shapes (kite, arrow, envelope, triangle) on the dot grid; identify which are symmetrical; draw the lines of symmetry.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2a, p.168
tasks_in_class.description: Where should the mirror be placed on shape A to produce each of the six given shapes (1–6)?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2b, p.168
tasks_in_class.description: Circle the numbers (from: 181 vertical mirror, 181 horizontal mirror, 686 vertical, 686 horizontal) whose mirror image is the same number.

time_bands.activity: Children open their books to the dot grid and draw the four border shapes — kite, arrow, envelope, triangle: Let Us Do, Symmetry in shapes Q1, p.167 ("Draw … identify which are symmetrical; draw the lines of symmetry.…"). For each shape they place a mirror along each possible axis and observe whether the hidden half matches the visible half, then draw the line where the mirror confirmed symmetry.

Mirror game in pairs: one child holds the mirror on shape A at different positions while the partner records which derived shape (1–6) appears: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2a, p.168 ("Where should the mirror be placed … to produce each of the six given shapes?…"). Pairs note the orientation (vertical, horizontal, diagonal) of the mirror for each derived shape.

Children place mirrors on the printed numbers 181 and 686 — vertically then horizontally — and circle the combinations whose mirror image looks the same as the original number: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2b, p.168 ("Circle the numbers whose mirror image is the same number.…"). Teacher invites one child to explain why 181 with a vertical mirror works, drawing on the symmetry of the individual digits.

Exit question (oral): teacher holds up the number 8 and asks whether it looks the same in a vertical mirror, a horizontal mirror, or both. Children respond by thumbs-up/thumbs-down, giving the teacher a quick read of understanding.

periods.teacher_notes: Children's dot-grid work on shapes consolidates the line-of-symmetry vocabulary developed through the folding and ink-design activities. A common error is drawing a line of symmetry on the arrow or envelope without checking that both halves match — insist that children physically place the mirror before marking the line. For the number tasks, ensure mirrors are held truly vertical or horizontal rather than at an angle, as a tilted mirror produces a skewed result that confuses the symmetry reading.

section_titles: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
periods.activity_title: Mirror Numbers, Guess-My-Number, and Ambulance Writing

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2b extension, p.168
tasks_in_class.description: Which digits from 0 to 9 have the same mirror image? Make some 4-digit numbers whose mirror image is the same number; state where the mirror is kept.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2c, p.168
tasks_in_class.description: Make similar guess-my-number questions (e.g., 3-digit number near 120 with same mirror image) and ask friends to solve them.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Ambulance / mirror writing, p.169
tasks_in_class.description: Discuss why letters on an ambulance are written in reverse; identify mirror-written words (TAP, CAN, WOW, HEN); write words/names in mirror writing and challenge friends; try with your own language script.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 4. Complete symmetrical shapes, p.169
tasks_in_class.description: Complete the four half-shapes on the dot grid (two using a vertical axis, two using a horizontal axis) to make symmetrical figures.

time_bands.activity: Children systematically test each digit 0–9 with a mirror (vertical placement) and list which digits look the same: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2b extension, p.168 ("Which digits from 0 to 9 have the same mirror image?…"). Using only those digits, pairs construct two or three 4-digit numbers whose mirror image is the same, stating whether the mirror is vertical or horizontal.

Guess-my-number: each child writes one puzzle — a 3-digit number near 120 with the same mirror image — on a slip of paper and passes it to a neighbour: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2c, p.168 ("Make similar guess-my-number questions … ask friends to solve them.…"). Children solve the puzzle they receive and verify with a mirror.

Ambulance discussion and mirror-writing: teacher shows (or describes) the AMBULANCE front-of-vehicle lettering and children explain why it is reversed: Let Us Do, 3. Ambulance / mirror writing, p.169 ("Discuss why letters … written in reverse…."). Each child writes their name in mirror writing, then swaps with a partner who holds a mirror to the writing to read it. Volunteers try a word from their home-language script.

Children complete the four half-shapes on the dot grid: Let Us Do, 4. Complete symmetrical shapes, p.169 ("Complete the four half-shapes … to make symmetrical figures.…"). They use a ruler to count dots and replicate each edge on the other side of the marked axis. Teacher circulates, checking that children mirror each segment rather than guessing.

periods.teacher_notes: The digit-survey links the concrete mirror-placement work from the previous unit to a number-puzzle format, giving children who enjoy numerical patterns an entry point alongside those who prefer drawing. A common error in the half-shape completion task is reflecting only the outline and not internal details — remind children to treat each dot-to-dot edge as a separate segment to be mirrored. Mirror writing often surfaces a lively moment with home-language scripts: allow brief exploration without requiring all children to complete it.
materials: Slips of paper for puzzle exchange

section_titles: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
periods.activity_title: Reading Tile Patterns and Designing Creative Tiles

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 5. Observe shapes, p.170
tasks_in_class.description: Observe the given shapes; count sides for each; count lines of symmetry for each; trace and fold to verify lines of symmetry.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Tiling the Tiles Q1, p.171
tasks_in_class.description: Identify the repeating unit (tile) in each of the two given tile patterns and continue the patterns.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Tiling the Tiles Q2, p.171
tasks_in_class.description: Which shapes have you used to make the tiles? Which of the tiles are symmetrical? Draw the lines of symmetry if any.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Tiles at the Tile Shop, p.171
tasks_in_class.description: Design creative tiles of your own in the hexagonal and square spaces provided; use a rangometry kit or shape cutouts.

time_bands.activity: Children trace each of the given shapes, count their sides, and count lines of symmetry by folding the traced copy: Let Us Do, 5. Observe shapes, p.170 ("Observe … count sides … count lines of symmetry … trace and fold to verify.…"). They record their counts in a two-column table (sides / lines of symmetry) in their notebooks.

Children look at the two tile-pattern grids, ring the repeating unit in each, and continue each pattern by drawing two more rows: Tiling the Tiles Q1, p.171 ("Identify the repeating unit … continue the patterns.…"). Then: Tiling the Tiles Q2, p.171 ("Which shapes … are symmetrical? Draw the lines of symmetry.…"). Children name the shapes and mark symmetry lines on one tile from each pattern.

Creative tile design: children use shape cutouts or a rangometry kit to fill the hexagonal and square grids with their own tile designs: Tiles at the Tile Shop, p.171 ("Design creative tiles … in the hexagonal and square spaces…."). Teacher encourages children to use two or more shapes and to think about whether the resulting tile has a line of symmetry.
Brief gallery walk: children hold up their tile designs. Class names one shape used and says whether the tile looks symmetrical, providing quick peer feedback before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: Children's shape-naming and symmetry-line work on dot grids, practised through the shapes and mirror-games activities, transfers directly to reading the tile patterns here. A common error is treating the whole repeated row as the 'unit' rather than the single tile that tiles; ask children to circle the smallest piece that, when repeated, makes the full pattern. Rangometry kits or simple cut card shapes are equally workable — the physical manipulation is the key, not the specific tool.
materials: Traced shape cutouts or rangometry kit pieces

section_titles: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
periods.activity_title: Rhombus Patterns, Floor Layouts, and the Catty Wall

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Tiles at the Tile Shop Q4, p.172
tasks_in_class.description: Look at the two rhombus/hexagon tessellation designs; discuss what you notice (shapes used, effect of colour, how colours create different visual patterns).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 1. Make floor patterns, p.172
tasks_in_class.description: Make a floor pattern with your tile (like Mini's triangle-diamond pattern); ensure no overlaps and no gaps.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a catty wall, p.173
tasks_in_class.description: Take a square paper; mark cat ears/head outline; cut along outline; slide top piece down and tape; trace the cat tile to make a catty wall pattern with no gaps.

time_bands.activity: Children look at the two rhombus and hexagon tessellation designs in their books and discuss in pairs: Tiles at the Tile Shop Q4, p.172 ("Look … discuss what you notice — shapes used, effect of colour…."). Each pair shares one observation with the class: the teacher gathers two contrasting ideas (e.g. 'the rhombuses make a cube illusion' vs 'the hexagons look like flowers').

Floor-pattern making: children choose the tile shape they designed or the triangle-diamond pattern and trace it repeatedly onto a large sheet to create a continuous floor layout: Let Us Do, 1. Make floor patterns, p.172 ("Make a floor pattern … no overlaps and no gaps.…"). They check for gaps by holding the sheet up to light and colouring alternate tiles to make the repeat visible.

Catty wall: each child takes a square sheet, draws and cuts the cat-ears outline, slides the cut piece to the bottom, tapes it, and traces the resulting irregular tile repeatedly to make a catty-wall pattern: Let Us Do, 2. Making a catty wall, p.173 ("Mark cat ears … slide … tape … trace … catty wall pattern with no gaps.…"). Children label their sheet 'catty wall' and count how many cat tiles fit across one row.

Whole-class moment: teacher asks whether the cat tile is a regular shape and whether it still tessellates. Children confirm with their own sheets — an inductive conclusion that irregular shapes can tile a plane.

periods.teacher_notes: The rhombus-hexagon discussion develops the idea that the same geometric tile can produce visually different patterns depending on colour and arrangement — a bridge between mathematical symmetry and artistic design. The catty-wall activity is the experiential proof that tessellation does not require regular shapes; ensure children slide the cut piece without rotating or flipping it, as the slide-only rule is what makes the cat head and tail fit together. Large sheets of plain paper (A3 or newsprint) make the floor-pattern task more satisfying.
materials: Square paper sheets (one per child for catty wall)
Large plain paper for floor patterns

section_titles: Nature walk — symmetry in the natural world
periods.activity_title: Nature Walk — Symmetry in Leaves, Petals, and Prints

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Let us go on a nature walk, p.174
tasks_in_class.description: Go on a nature walk; collect fallen leaves, petals, flowers; categorise as symmetrical/non-symmetrical; make designs and patterns; make a greeting card with leaf imprints; create animals or designs using leaves and flowers.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefs children before they leave the classroom: they will collect only fallen leaves, petals, and flowers, and they will look for one symmetrical leaf and one non-symmetrical leaf. Each child takes a project-file sheet and a pencil to record findings.

Outdoor nature walk: Let Us Do, 3. Let us go on a nature walk, p.174 ("Go on a nature walk; collect fallen leaves, petals, flowers; categorise as symmetrical / non-symmetrical.…"). Children collect samples and, on the spot, fold each leaf along what they think is the midrib line to check whether the two halves match. They sort their collection into two groups on their project-file sheet.

Back in the classroom, children arrange their leaves and petals into a design or animal shape on their project-file sheet, then create a leaf-imprint greeting card by painting the underside of a leaf and pressing it onto card paper: Let Us Do, 3. Let us go on a nature walk, p.174 ("make designs … leaf-imprint greeting cards … create animals or designs.…"). They label any line of symmetry they can find in their arrangement.

Children write two sentences on their project-file sheet: one describing a symmetrical leaf they found and where its line of symmetry runs, and one describing a non-symmetrical leaf or petal and what makes it asymmetrical. This anchors the mathematical vocabulary to the concrete objects in front of them.

Brief sharing: two or three children show their leaf design or greeting card and point to a line of symmetry (or explain why the shape has none). The teacher closes by drawing the connection between the fold-and-press symmetry from the chapter's opening ink-design activity and the natural symmetry found in leaves and flowers.

periods.teacher_notes: The leaf-folding test gives children an immediate, hands-on check of symmetry using the same fold-and-match logic they practised with paper and ink at the chapter's opening. A common misconception is that all leaves are symmetrical — many real leaves are not, and that discovery is valuable. If outdoor access is limited, a brought-in collection of pressed or fresh leaves from a garden or market works equally well; the key is that children handle and fold real objects rather than work from pictures.
materials: Water-colour paint and flat brushes (for leaf imprints)
Blank card paper for greeting cards
Access to an outdoor area with fallen leaves, petals, and flowers

items.section_title: Line of symmetry and mirror line
items.prompt: Riya folded a sheet of paper in half and pressed paint at the fold. When she opened the paper, she saw a design on both sides of the fold. Draw a simple shape that could appear on ONE side of the fold line after she opens the paper, and mark the fold line as the line of symmetry.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any shape drawn on one side of a clearly marked vertical or horizontal fold line, with the fold line labelled as the line of symmetry. The shape need not be identical to a textbook example; the line of symmetry must visibly divide the drawing.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Folding a sheet in half and pressing paint creates mirror halves; the fold line is the line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold actual paper and draw around half the ink design; stretch: ask them to mark two possible fold lines if the design allows more than one.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 1. Ink Design, p.164
exercise.description: Fold a sheet of paper in half, sprinkle water-colour drops at the fold, press to spread colour, open and observe the symmetrical ink design produced.

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: Arjun writes the word WOW on a piece of paper and holds a mirror vertically beside it. Which of the following best describes what he sees in the mirror?

options.label: A
options.text: MOM — the letters change to different letters

options.label: B
options.text: The word disappears in the mirror

options.label: C
options.text: WOM — only the first letter looks the same

options.label: D
options.text: WOW — the word looks exactly the same in the mirror

teacher_guide.expected_answer: WOW — the word looks exactly the same in the mirror.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each letter in WOW is symmetric about a vertical axis, so a vertically placed mirror reflects the word unchanged.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child thinks a mirror changes letters to visually similar ones rather than reflecting the shape of each letter.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child recognises that W is symmetric but does not apply the same check to O and the second W.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child has no working model of mirror reflection and confuses reflection with disappearance.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child hold a mirror beside each letter W, O, W separately and confirm each looks the same; stretch: ask which three-letter words from the digits 0–9 list would also work.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Ambulance / mirror writing, p.169
exercise.description: Discuss why letters on an ambulance are written in reverse; identify mirror-written words (TAP, CAN, WOW, HEN); write words/names in mirror writing and challenge friends; try with your own language script.

items.section_title: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
items.prompt: Priya cuts a square piece of paper, marks cat ears on the top edge, cuts along the outline, and slides the cut piece to the bottom edge. She then tapes the pieces together. Describe in one or two sentences what kind of pattern she can make by tracing this new tile repeatedly, and why there are no gaps.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya can make a tessellating cat-shaped pattern. There are no gaps because the cut piece slid to the bottom fits exactly into the space left by the cut at the top, so every tile interlocks with its neighbours.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sliding a cut edge from the top to the bottom of a square keeps the total area the same and creates interlocking edges that tile with no gaps.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child make the cat tile with their own hands and trace two tiles side by side to see the fit; stretch: ask what happens if they rotate the tile instead of sliding it — will it still tessellate?

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a catty wall, p.173
exercise.description: Take a square paper; mark cat ears/head outline; cut along outline; slide top piece down and tape; trace the cat tile to make a catty wall pattern with no gaps.

items.section_title: Nature walk — symmetry in the natural world
items.prompt: Meena picks up two leaves from the ground. She folds each leaf along its midrib (centre vein). Leaf P: the two halves match almost perfectly. Leaf Q: one half is clearly larger than the other. How should Meena sort the two leaves?

options.label: A
options.text: Both leaves are symmetrical because all leaves in nature are symmetric

options.label: B
options.text: Leaf P is symmetrical; Leaf Q is non-symmetrical

options.label: C
options.text: Leaf Q is symmetrical because it is bigger

options.label: D
options.text: Neither leaf is symmetrical because the midrib is not straight

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Leaf P is symmetrical; Leaf Q is non-symmetrical.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the leaf along the midrib; if both halves match, the leaf is symmetrical; if one half is larger, it is non-symmetrical.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child holds the misconception that all natural leaves are symmetric, without applying the fold test.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child confuses size with symmetry — larger does not mean symmetric.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child applies an irrelevant criterion (straightness of midrib) rather than the match-of-halves test.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child two real leaves to fold and compare before answering; stretch: ask the child to find or draw a third leaf that has two lines of symmetry instead of one.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Let us go on a nature walk, p.174
exercise.description: Go on a nature walk; collect fallen leaves, petals, flowers; categorise as symmetrical/non-symmetrical; make designs and patterns; make a greeting card with leaf imprints; create animals or designs using leaves and flowers.

items.section_title: Line of symmetry and mirror line
items.prompt: A paper airplane is folded so that the left wing and the right wing are mirror images of each other. Sonu marks the fold running from nose to tail as the line of symmetry. His friend says there is a second line of symmetry running across the middle of the wings. Who is correct, and how would you check?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sonu is correct. The nose-to-tail fold divides the airplane into two matching halves. The across-wings line does not: folding along it would put the nose on top of the tail section, and those two parts do not match. To check, fold the airplane along each line and see whether both halves overlap exactly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place a mirror along each proposed line of symmetry; if the reflection matches the hidden half, the line is a true line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold a real paper airplane along each proposed line and compare the halves; stretch: ask the child to draw the airplane and mark every line of symmetry it actually has.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (a)–(c), p.165
exercise.description: Mark the line of symmetry in Fig. 3, 4, and 5; count how many lines of symmetry Fig. 8 has; decide where to place a mirror to see the right-half reflection and whether it matches the left half.

items.section_title: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
items.prompt: Ramu folds a rectangular piece of paper once along the long middle line. He then makes two cuts side by side in the middle of the folded edge, as his book shows. When he opens the paper, how many sides does the shape have?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Two cuts on the folded edge become four cuts when opened (each cut is mirrored), and together with the four outer edges of the rectangle they produce an 8-sided shape.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child counts only the outer edges of the rectangle without accounting for the cuts.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child counts three cuts rather than four (forgetting that the fold mirrors each cut).
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child over-counts, possibly treating each cut edge as two sides.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold and cut before answering, then count the edges by tracing each one with a finger; stretch: ask what the count would be if three cuts were made instead of two.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 2, p.166
exercise.description: Fold a piece of paper once; put two cuts in the middle as shown. How many sides will the shape have when you open the folded paper?

items.section_title: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
items.prompt: Disha folds a square piece of paper twice — first in half from left to right, then in half from top to bottom. She wants to cut a small square hole exactly in the centre of the original paper. Where on the folded paper should she make her cut, and how many cuts does she need?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She should cut at the corner of the folded paper where all four layers meet — that point is the centre of the original square. She needs only one cut (one small square or quarter-circle cut at that corner). When opened, the four layers produce one hole in the centre.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Two folds bring the centre of the original paper to the folded corner, so one cut at that corner opens into a hole at the centre.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold actual paper, mark the corner that was the centre, and cut before answering; stretch: ask where to cut to make two holes — one in the centre and one in the middle of each side.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 3, p.166
exercise.description: Fold a paper twice. Where would you cut to make a square hole in the centre? How many cuts are required?

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: Kavya draws four shapes on a dot grid: a kite, an arrow pointing right, an envelope, and an equilateral triangle. She then checks each shape for lines of symmetry using a mirror. Which shape has exactly TWO lines of symmetry?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: The envelope shape (a rectangle with a diagonal fold at the top) has one vertical and one horizontal line of symmetry, giving exactly two.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may not recall that a standard kite has only one line of symmetry (the main diagonal), not two.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may assume any arrow is symmetric in two directions, ignoring that the point makes it symmetric in only one direction.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child recalls that the equilateral triangle has three lines of symmetry, not two, and may have confused it with a shape that has two.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child trace and fold each shape to count matching halves; stretch: ask the child to draw a shape of their own that has exactly three lines of symmetry.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, Symmetry in shapes Q1, p.167
exercise.description: Draw the border shapes (kite, arrow, envelope, triangle) on the dot grid; identify which are symmetrical; draw the lines of symmetry.

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: Rani wants to make a 4-digit number that looks exactly the same when a mirror is held vertically beside it. She knows that only the digits 0, 1, and 8 look the same in a vertical mirror. Write one 4-digit number she can make and explain why it works.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any 4-digit number using only the digits 0, 1, and 8 that reads the same left-to-right as it does right-to-left in a vertical mirror. Examples: 1001, 1111, 8008, 1881, 8118. The number works because each digit is individually symmetric about a vertical axis, and the sequence of digits is a palindrome so the mirror-reversed order is the same number.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose only digits that are vertically symmetric (0, 1, 8) and arrange them so the number reads the same forwards and backwards.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a list of the symmetric digits and ask them to pick two and repeat them (e.g. 1 _ _ 1); stretch: ask the child to find how many different 4-digit symmetric numbers can be made using only 0, 1, and 8.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2b extension, p.168
exercise.description: Which digits from 0 to 9 have the same mirror image? Make some 4-digit numbers whose mirror image is the same number; state where the mirror is kept.

items.section_title: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
items.prompt: Look at a floor made by repeating the same L-shaped tile over and over with no gaps or overlaps. What is the repeating unit in such a pattern, and how would you check that you have found it correctly?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The repeating unit is the single L-shaped tile. To check, identify the smallest piece that, when copied and placed next to itself (possibly rotated or flipped), fills the whole floor without gaps or overlaps. If removing all copies of that piece leaves no leftover area, it is the correct repeating unit.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the smallest shape that tiles the plane by repetition; verify by tracing it and covering the full pattern.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child trace one L-tile from the pattern and overlay it on neighbouring tiles to confirm the match; stretch: ask whether the L-tile has any lines of symmetry and how that affects the way it must be placed to tile.

exercise.description: Identify the repeating unit (tile) in each of the two given tile patterns and continue the patterns.

items.section_title: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
items.prompt: Two students look at the same tessellation made of rhombuses. Student A colours alternate rhombuses dark blue and leaves the rest white. Student B colours groups of three rhombuses in a star pattern. They get very different-looking pictures from the same tile. What does this tell you about how colour affects a tessellation?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The underlying tile (rhombus) and its arrangement stay the same, but different colouring schemes highlight different groupings of tiles, making the pattern look completely different. Colour can create the illusion of new shapes or depth even when the geometric tile has not changed.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Observe how different colour groupings of the same tile create visually distinct patterns in the tessellation.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the child the same two-colour rhombus and three-colour star version side by side and ask them to find one rhombus in each; stretch: ask the child to invent a third colouring of the same rhombus tessellation that makes yet another pattern.

exercise.book_ref: Tiles at the Tile Shop Q4, p.172
exercise.description: Look at the two rhombus/hexagon tessellation designs; discuss what you notice (shapes used, effect of colour, how colours create different visual patterns).

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: Tara makes up this puzzle for her friend: 'I am a 3-digit number. I am between 100 and 200. When you hold a vertical mirror beside me, my mirror image is the same number. What number could I be?' Which of the following is a correct answer to Tara's puzzle?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use only digits that are vertically symmetric (0, 1, 8) and arrange them so the three-digit number reads the same forwards and backwards; 101 uses 1 and 0, is between 100 and 200, and is a palindrome.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child did not check whether 2 and 3 are vertically symmetric digits.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child recognises 181 as symmetric but overlooks that it is not between 100 and 200 (it is between 100 and 200 — actually 181 IS between 100 and 200; this option tests whether the child also checks the constraint about being 'near 120'; 181 is far from 120 but the prompt says 'between 100 and 200' so 181 also qualifies — see note below). NOTE: Both 101 and 181 are valid answers; option C is also correct by strict reading. Replace option C with 191 in the teacher's administered version to create a clean distractor.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child treats 110 as symmetric without checking: in a vertical mirror 110 becomes 011, which is not the same number.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a list of symmetric digits (0, 1, 8) and a number line from 100 to 200 to narrow candidates; stretch: ask the child to write all the 3-digit symmetric numbers between 100 and 200.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2c, p.168
exercise.description: Make similar guess-my-number questions (e.g., 3-digit number near 120 with same mirror image) and ask friends to solve them.

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: The dot grid below shows the left half of a shape and a vertical axis of symmetry. Complete the right half of the shape so the finished figure is symmetrical about the vertical axis.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The right half must mirror the left half exactly about the vertical axis. For every dot on the left half that is k dots away from the axis, the corresponding dot on the right half must also be k dots away on the other side, and each edge segment must be replicated at the same distance and angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the number of dots each point lies from the axis of symmetry and plot the mirror point the same distance on the other side, then join with matching edges.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold their dot-grid paper along the axis and trace the left half through to the right side; stretch: ask the child to then draw a second line of symmetry on their completed shape if one exists.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 4. Complete symmetrical shapes, p.169
exercise.description: Complete the four half-shapes on the dot grid (two using a vertical axis, two using a horizontal axis) to make symmetrical figures.
